note: The 24 checkpoint-after-exhibits documents judged in one sitting immediately after the before set (2026-09-08-rejudge-checkpoint-before-4.json); compare `now` against that file.

then.rationale: Integrity and legibility hold: no clipping, overlap or placeholder text anywhere; body copy on pages 2–3 is a readable size with strong contrast, and the single-column reading order is unambiguous. Coherence is genuinely good — the blue rule under each H1 ("Share erosion is accelerating...", "Two repositioning paths...", "Recommend premiumising...", "Evidence that would change this recommendation"), the running head "Repositioning Assessment", and the "Confidential / page / date" footer repeat identically on pages 2, 3 and 4, and the cover's accent rule above "Marketing Director" ties back to it. Where it fails is level 4, density and structure. Page 4 is roughly three-quarters empty white: three short paragraphs of continuation, a "Notes and sources" list of two items, and then nothing to the footer. On a four-page deliverable that means a quarter of the document is a stub, and it reads as an overrun rather than a designed closing page — the notes should have sat at the foot of page 3 or the recommendation should have been given room to fill page 4. Two smaller level-4 gaps: the assessment contains no chart at all, only the narrow-gap/premiumise table on page 3 and the 4 pts / 38% / 61% stat row beneath it, so a share-erosion trend that the whole argument rests on is asserted in prose only; and the table's "Volume" row carries "Flat" and "-15%" without stating over what period. On distinctiveness, the content is clearly written for this brief, but the visual language — thin blue rule, plain unruled table with a grey header band, three oversized figures in a row — would look identical on any category-strategy memo; nothing about the composition says heritage food brand.

Integrity and legibility hold: no placeholder text, body copy is a readable size, and the single-column reading order is unambiguous. Coherence is decent — the blue rule under each section heading, the running header ('Repositioning Assessment: Defending Share Against Private Label'), and the three-part footer (Client Confidential / page x of 4 / 8 September 2026) repeat on pages 2-4. Where it stops short of level 4 is communicative fit. The brief is quantitative — 4 points of share lost over three years, a price gap widening to 38%, 61% of growth from under-40s — and the document contains no chart at all; the only visual devices are one comparison table and the KPI trio (-4.0 / 38% / 61%) on page 3. That table, 'Modelled three-year outlook, by repositioning option', is also crowded hard against the right margin: the 'Premiumise' column header and its values (83.0, +4.0, +7.0) sit at the very edge of the text block, unlike every paragraph above it, so the option the document is recommending is the least comfortably set element on the page. Pacing is uneven too: the page 1 cover leaves the bottom two-thirds entirely empty with no mark other than the title block, and page 4 stops a third of the way down after 'Notes and sources', so the four-page arc ends on a stub. Small stray marks appear under the header on pages 2 and 3 and between paragraphs — minor, but they read as artifacts rather than intent. Positives worth crediting: the section titles are conclusions, not labels ('Matching private label's price will not win back share', 'Private label wins on relevance, not on distrust of the brand', 'The recommendation holds until growth or trust shift first'), the table carries a source line, and the numbers carry units (pts, %). The look is defensible but the system — plain single column, one accent rule, a KPI band, a 'Note on this research' box — would sit unchanged under any consulting memo; only the words are specific to this heritage brand.

Integrity and legibility hold: no clipping, no placeholder text, footers ('Confidential / 2-4 / 9 September 2026') and the blue rule + 'Repositioning Assessment' eyebrow repeat identically on pages 2-4, and the type sizes and blue accent are consistent throughout, so level 3 is met. Level 4 is not. Page 4 is the clearest failure: the closing recommendation-review paragraphs and the two-item 'Notes and sources' list stop about 40% down the page, leaving well over half the sheet blank with no closing device — the document trails off rather than ends. Second, the section headings are labels rather than conclusions: 'Situation' (p2), 'The choice' (p2) and 'Recommendation' (p3) tell the marketing director nothing on their own, when the page-3 argument ('premiumise rather than chase price') is exactly the kind of sentence the heading should carry. Third, for a brief built on 4 points of share loss over three years and a 38% price gap, there is no chart anywhere in four pages — the quantitative spine is carried entirely by the page-3 three-column option table and the 4pts/38%/61% KPI strip. Both of those are well handled (units on every figure, arrows on the deltas, and a 'Company share, pricing and shopper segmentation data, 2026' source line under each), which is why this reads as a competent memo, not a broken one. There are also small stray glyph marks at the top of the text column on pages 2 and 3 (below the running head, and again between 'Situation' and the body) that look like leftover characters rather than intended labels. Not generic in content — the page-2 callout 'Two paths, not two tactics' and the page-3 heading 'What would change this recommendation' are written for this brief — but the visual system (thin blue rule, eyebrow, plain serif body, rule-under-heading) is the default consulting memo dress and would look identical for any other client.

Integrity and legibility hold: no clipping, no placeholders, footers and page numbers repeat on pages 2-4, and the reading order is unambiguous. Visual coherence is genuine — the blue rule above/below each H2 ('Where the programme stands', 'What is recoverable this quarter', 'The three decisions'), the small-caps eyebrow labels, and the running header repeat exactly across pages. It stops at level 3 on density fit. Page 2 ends after a single paragraph under 'Delivery by workstream' at roughly two-thirds down, leaving the bottom third of the page blank with no visual reason — in a four-page review that empty band reads as a page the author abandoned rather than a deliberate break, and it is the reason I would not send it. Page 4 has the same softer problem: 'Notes and sources' closes around three-quarters down. Secondary issues: the KPI row on page 2 renders the currency as '19€m' / '28€m' with the euro glyph trailing the figure instead of '€19m', which is wrong in every one of the three stats; and the section titles are labels rather than conclusions — 'Where the programme stands' and 'Delivery by workstream' state the topic, where the body underneath already contains the finding ('the programme lands near EUR 33m, EUR 13m short'). Credit where due for level 4 attributes that are present: the page 3 bar chart carries an axis unit ('Delivery vs target (%)'), a numbered figure caption with a stated takeaway, and a PMO source line; the three-decision table names Head CRE, CIO and Sponsor against 1.8/1.5/1.2 EUR m with its own source line. Not generic in substance — the decision table, the 118%/41%/33% split and the 72%-of-target landing figure could only belong to this brief — but the shell (blue accent, three-up stat row, rule-bracketed headings) is a common corporate report chassis.

Content and structure are the strongest part of this: page 2's H1 "The shortfall sits in two workstreams, not the whole programme" and page 3's "Half the €9m shortfall is recoverable this quarter" are conclusions, not labels; the page 3 table carries proper units in its column heads (Target €m, Delivered %) with a Programme Management Office source line beneath it; the €19m / €28m / €46m stat trio is also sourced; the decisions are numbered with named owners (Head of Corporate Real Estate, CIO, COO as Programme Sponsor); and "Notes and sources" closes the document. What keeps it below level 4 is a small integrity blemish that repeats: a stray two-character mark sits in the slot immediately above the H1 on page 2, above the H1 on page 3, and again above "Three decisions this quarter, three named owners" on page 3 — an eyebrow/kicker that has rendered as a stub rather than as a label, and it appears in exactly the same position each time, so a reader sees it three times. The cover is also underweight: the rule, "Transformation Office", "Cost Programme Review", the month/date lines and the confidentiality line all sit in a band across the middle third, leaving the top quarter and the bottom half of page 1 empty with nothing to anchor them — the €46m/€19m headline that drives the whole review never appears on the cover. Elsewhere the system holds: consistent running header and three-part footer, one blue accent used on the cover rule and the table header rule, callout treatment on page 2 ("Why 'unowned' is the right word") reading as a deliberate device. Genericness is middling rather than high: the numbers, workstream names and owner titles are specific to this brief and the stat trio is a considered choice, but the visual language — hairline rule, single blue accent, default sans, plain three-column table — would transfer unchanged to any other programme review, and there is no chart anywhere to carry the 118% / 41% / 33% contrast that the argument turns on.

Integrity and legibility hold: no clipping, no placeholders, running header/footer and page numbers are consistent on pages 2-4, and the reading order is unambiguous. Coherence is good — the blue rule under the section titles, the stat band on page 2, and the figure/table caption-plus-source pattern on page 3 all repeat cleanly. Communicatively it does the brief's work: section titles are conclusions rather than labels ("What is driving the shortfall", "The decisions that unlock recovery", "What this programme will land at if nothing changes"), the page 3 bar chart carries both a takeaway caption (procurement over-delivering while property and IT sit below 45%) and a source line, and the decisions table gives value in EUR m and a decide-by date per row. Level 5 fails on three visible craft defects. First, the page 2 stat band renders currency as "19€m" and "4.5€m" — the euro sign trails the figure in a superscript position, which is wrong for a EUR document and is the most prominent typography on the page. Second, page 4 opens with a dense run-in paragraph that re-lists the same three decisions as inline numbered text ("1) Exit two leased floors... 2) Retire legacy platform... 3) Raise the delegated sign-off limit"), duplicating the page 3 table in a form that is much harder to scan and reading as an orphan from the previous page. Third, page 4 stops roughly 40% down — the "Notes and sources" list ends mid-page and over half the final page is blank, so the document trails off rather than closing. Not shippable unchanged: fix the euro glyph placement in the stat band, cut or restructure the duplicated decisions paragraph, and rebalance the last page. Genericness is low-to-moderate — the stat band, decision table and workstream chart are shaped by this brief, but the blue-rule-over-heading treatment and cover layout would sit unchanged on any transformation-office report.

Integrity holds: no clipping, no placeholder text, the page 3/4 table split repeats its header row ("Readiness tier / Datapoints / Share of total") on page 4 rather than orphaning it. Legibility is fine at print size — the body text on page 2 and the 34/82 · 29/82 · 19/82 KPI trio have clear contrast and an obvious top-to-bottom reading order, and the running header/footer ("CSRD Readiness Assessment" / "Confidential — Audit Committee", page x of 4, 9 September 2026) repeats identically on pages 2–4. Coherence holds too: the same blue rule under the H1, the same italic source line under every exhibit (KPI trio, Figure 1, the readiness-tier table), the same left margin on all pages. Communicatively it is genuinely good for an audit-committee brief — every heading states a conclusion rather than a topic ("The Manufacturer Can Source Two-Thirds of Required Datapoints Today", "Scope 3 Emissions Remain the Largest Unmeasured Risk", "The First Report Will Disclose Gaps, Not Hide Them"), the page 3 bar chart carries a unit on the y-axis ("Measurement maturity (0–5, internal)") and a caption that reads as a takeaway ("Scope 3 is a build project, not a reporting task"), and the page 4 methodology note pre-empts the obvious audit-committee challenge about the ±19 datapoint boundary. Level 5 is where it stops: page 1 is a near-empty cover with the title block sitting at roughly a third height and the remaining two-thirds blank, and page 3 breaks the readiness-tier table after a single data row ("Already collected / 34 / 41.5%"), pushing the other two tiers onto page 4 — both read as default flow rather than composed pages. Visually it is a competent but unremarkable blue-accent report shell; the numbers and headings are unmistakably about this 82-datapoint gap analysis, but the type, rules and exhibit furniture would look identical on any other subject.

Integrity and legibility hold: no clipping, no placeholder text, consistent running head ("CSRD Readiness Assessment") and footer ("Strictly Confidential / page / 9 September 2026") on pages 2-4, and a single obvious column reading order. Communicative effectiveness is genuinely good: every heading states a conclusion rather than a topic ("Scope 3 emissions are the largest unmeasured gap", "The first report will state estimates, not certainty"), the page 3 bar chart carries a numbered caption, a takeaway line and a source line, its y-axis is labelled "Datapoints (of 82)", the page 3 table has a header row, a Target column with quarters and its own source, and the page 2 KPI trio (34 / 29 / 19) is labelled and sourced. What stops it short of level 5, and stops me sending it: page 4 ends about a third of the way down — the estimation callout, one heading, one paragraph and a two-item "Notes and sources" list leave two-thirds of the sheet blank, so the document trails off rather than closing. Page 1 is also very light, with the title block sitting in the top quarter and nothing else on the page. Content-wise the audit committee gets one chart and one three-row gap table for a 19-datapoint build programme — no owners, no cost, no sequenced timeline beyond the Q1/Q2/Q4 targets. There are also small unexplained numerals floating between blocks on pages 2 and 3 (above the first heading and between the KPI band and the "41%" section) that read as stray marks rather than intentional numbering. Genericness: the content is unmistakably this brief, but the shell — thin blue rule under each heading, three-up big-number band, one blue bar chart, one bordered mini-table — is the default corporate report dress and would look identical for a pricing review or an IT audit.

Integrity holds: no clipping, no placeholders, the page-3 bar chart, its caption and the three-row disclosure-area table all render fully, and the numbers reconcile (26+6+2 = 34 collected; 41/35/23% maps to 34/29/19 of 82). Legibility is adequate — the blue rule, running header and 'Confidential — Audit Committee' footer with page numbers repeat identically on pages 2–4, and reading order is unambiguous. Coherence is met: the KPI trio on page 2, the figure caption on page 3 and the callout on page 4 share one type scale and one accent blue.

It stops short of level 4 on structure and density. Page 4 carries the whole ask of the brief — what to build first, what to estimate, what the report cannot say — as five undifferentiated prose paragraphs with no subheads, no numbering and no table, so the three workstreams named in the first sentence ('first, second, third') are buried mid-paragraph rather than scannable by an audit committee; the page then stops two-thirds down under a 'Notes and sources' list with a single entry, leaving a visible stub. Page 1 is also thin: title, subtitle, date and confidentiality line sit in the top third and the remaining two-thirds of the cover are empty, with no indication of the headline finding the document actually leads with. Page 2's 'Key takeaways' bullets and the 41%/35%/23% stat row do the job well, which makes the contrast with page 4 sharper.

Genericness: the titles are argued rather than labelled ('Readiness is real but partial, and Scope 3 is the gap'), and the table and chart are built from this brief's numbers, so it is not blank-filling. But the shell — cover with a rule, KPI trio, one chart page, one prose page — is a stock report frame that would carry any other assessment unchanged.

I would not send page 4 to an audit committee in this form.

Integrity and legibility hold: nothing is clipped or placeholdered, the FY2026–FY2028 bar chart on p3 has a figure caption, a stated takeaway and a source line, and the KPI trio on p2 (340 €m / 9% / 61%) carries units and captions. Repeated furniture is consistent — the running head 'Nordic Market Entry Assessment', the page x/5 and 9 September 2026 footer, and the thin blue rules under each section heading are identical on pages 2–5 — so visual coherence is met. Level 4 fails on density and flow. The 'Nordic market structure and Finnish-language coverage, 2026' table breaks across the p3/p4 boundary and leaves a single orphaned row ('New entrant (pre-entry) / 0% / Planned') plus a repeated header and its source note alone at the top of p4, which is the weakest thing in the document. Page 5 is roughly one-third filled: 'Conditions for Success' with its three bullets and the four-item 'Notes and sources' list end above the midpoint and the remaining two-thirds of the page is blank, so the report trails off rather than closing. The cover on p1 is also thin — an eyebrow, title, one subtitle line, date and confidentiality line stacked at a third height with nothing else on the sheet. Section titles are labels, not conclusions ('Market Opportunity', 'Competitive Landscape', 'Economics of Entry'), which costs the communicative bar further. Genericness: the prose is entirely brief-specific (Finnish-language gap, Stockholm office, month 26 vs month 34 breakeven), but the container — blue-rule headings, one single-series bar chart, two plain header-row tables, one tinted callout — is a stock report shell that would look identical for any market-entry brief.

Integrity holds on all three pages: no clipping, no overflow, no placeholder text; the page-3 metrics table (Investment EUR m 2.1/2.1, Break-even month 26.0/34.0, Market growth 9.0%/9.0%) is fully drawn with both case columns and a source line under it. Legibility is fine at A4 body size, and the running header/footer pair (short title top-left, 'Confidential — Board Use Only' + page number + date bottom) repeats identically on pages 2 and 3. Coherence is consistent: the same thin accent rule under the cover title reappears under each page title, headings share one sans family and weight step, and the bulleted 'Key takeaways' box, the italic 'Definition: served vs. addressable' callout and the numbered 'Notes and sources' list all sit on the same left margin. Communicatively it does the brief's work: titles are conclusions ('Enter the Nordic Market via a Stockholm Office', 'Two Incumbents Dominate, Leaving Finland Unserved', 'The Business Case Pays Back Within the Investment Horizon'), the three conditions are named in prose under their own heading, and every figure carries a unit — EUR340m market size, 9%/yr growth, 61% incumbent combined share in the KPI trio, each with its own caption and a source line. Two things keep it off level 5: the payback is shown only as two numbers in a table row — there is no chart of the base vs downside cumulative curve the brief asks to 'show', so the single most decision-relevant comparison is the least visual thing on page 3; and the cover is thin, with the title block sitting in the upper third and the lower half of page 1 entirely empty. Not generic in content — the Finnish-language gap, the month-26/month-34 split and the Stockholm build-out are argued specifically — but the shell (rule, sans title, KPI trio, notes list) would look identical for any other market-entry brief.

Integrity holds: no clipping, overlap or placeholder text anywhere across the four pages, and the page-2/3 headers and footers ('Confidential — Board Use', page x of y, 3 September 2026) repeat consistently. Type is legible and the single-column reading order is unambiguous, and the page-3 statistic trio (340€m / 9% annual growth / 61% incumbent share) with its 'Market sizing and competitor share, internal analysis, Sep 2026' source line is a genuinely well-set element. Coherence is achieved: the same rule-under-heading treatment on 'Recommendation', 'Market Opportunity', 'Entry Economics and Payback' and 'Conditions the Recommendation Depends On', consistent margins, and the tinted 'Methodology' aside on page 2 all agree.

It fails level 4 on three counts. First, page 4 is a stub: it carries a single orphaned half-sentence ('management's control to deliver. We recommend the board approve entry.') and a two-item 'Notes and sources' list, leaving roughly 85% of the page blank — a board pack should not break the closing recommendation across a near-empty final page. Second, the brief asked to show payback under both cases, and the only artefact is the four-row page-3 table (Investment, Payback (months), Delta vs base); a payback/cumulative-cash curve comparing month 26 and month 34 is the one visual this document exists to show, and there is no chart on any page. Third, every heading names a topic rather than a conclusion — 'Market Opportunity', 'Risks and Mitigations', 'Conclusion' — so a board member skimming the headings learns nothing; the actual finding (Finland is unserved, entry pays back in 26 months) never surfaces above body text. Minor: '340€m' places the currency symbol after the numeral, inconsistent with 'EUR 340 million' used in the page-2 body.

Genericness: the cover (thin blue rule, 'Board of Directors' eyebrow, title, subtitle, date, confidentiality line) and the heading/aside system would be identical for any other consulting deliverable; only the numbers change. The statistic trio and methodology box lift it above a bare template, but nothing about the typography or composition is specific to a market-entry assessment.

Integrity holds: nothing clipped, no placeholders, the page 3 table header repeats correctly at the top of page 4, and the bar chart on page 3 renders with axis, legend and labels intact. Legibility is adequate but not generous — body type on pages 2-4 runs a very wide single-column measure at what looks like ~9pt, and the small-caps figure/source lines under the chart on page 3 and under the KPI row on page 2 sit near the floor of comfortable reading. Coherence is genuinely good: the blue rule under each H2, the running header 'Post-Merger Integration Assessment', and the three-part footer (confidential / page / date) repeat identically on pages 2-4; the KPI row on page 2 (31% / 12/41 / €8.2m) and the table on pages 3-4 share the same rule weights. Communicatively it does the job the brief set: every heading is a conclusion rather than a label ('Sequencing Determines Whether the Full Synergy Is Ever Captured' on page 2, 'Deferring the Migration a Year Forfeits Most of the Synergy' on page 4), the chart on page 3 carries a numbered caption, a one-line takeaway and a source, the milestone table names months 6/12/18 with synergy in €m and depots closed, and the 'Unfunded Dependency' callout on page 4 puts the unbudgeted €3.3m migration where the committee cannot miss it. What keeps it off level 5 is flow craft: page 2 stops roughly a fifth short of the bottom after the single paragraph under the 'Sequencing' heading, page 4 ends around 60% down after the notes list, and the milestone table breaks with only the Month 6 row on page 3 and the remaining two rows on page 4 — an avoidable orphan for a three-row table. The cover on page 1 is correct but bare: eyebrow, title, subtitle, date and confidentiality line all sit in the top third with nothing below.

Integrity and legibility hold: no clipped text, no placeholders, headers/footers ('Confidential — Steering Committee', page x/5, 9 September 2026) repeat on pages 2–5 and the single-column measure with a blue accent rule under each section heading is consistent. Communicatively it is strong for a steering committee: page 2's headline 'Synergy is real but two-fifths depends on an unbudgeted system' states a conclusion rather than a topic, the KPI band (31% customer overlap, 12/41 overlapping depots, 3.3 €m needing the dispatch system) carries units and a source line, page 3's Figure 1 line chart has both an explicit takeaway caption ('A twelve-month delay in approving the dispatch migration pushes full EUR8.2m run-rate capture from month twenty-four to month thirty-six') and a source, page 4's checkpoint table gives run-rate €m against % of target with a source, and the month 0–6 / 7–12 / 13–18 milestone bands answer the brief's sequencing question. Where it falls down is craft: page 5 is an orphan stub — one continuation paragraph and a single 'Notes and sources' entry, leaving roughly three-quarters of the page empty, so the document ends on visible dead space rather than a closing recommendation. Page 2 also runs two long unbroken body paragraphs after the KPI band with no visual relief, and page 4 pushes a bulleted milestone list, a table, a 'Why month one matters' aside and a new section heading onto one page, so density is uneven across the deck. Cover page 1 is sparse: a rule, title, subtitle and three small lines in the upper third with no other structure. Visually it is a competent but stock consulting report — accent rule, KPI trio, one line chart, one table — with nothing about the facilities/depot subject reflected in the design; the content is tailored, the composition would look identical for any other integration brief.

Integrity holds: no clipping, no placeholder text, the page-3 bar chart and the Month 6/12/18 synergy table both render fully inside the text column, and the running header/footer ("Integration Assessment: Acquisition of a Regional Competitor" / "Strictly Confidential — x of 4 — 9 September 2026") repeats cleanly on pages 2-4. Legibility is fine at report scale and reading order is unambiguous. Coherence is genuinely good: the blue rule under every H2, the same left-aligned heading weight on pages 2, 3 and 4, the figure caption + takeaway + source triplet under the chart mirrored by the caption + source pair under the table, and the 31% / 12/41 / 8.2€m stat band on page 2 all read as one system rather than hand-placed. Communicatively it does the brief's work: every heading states a conclusion ("40% of the synergy depends on one unfunded system decision", "Fund the dispatch decision on day one to unlock EUR 8.2m", "A one-year delay forfeits EUR 3.3m a year and heightens facility risk"), the chart carries an explicit takeaway ("The gap between the lines is about EUR 3.3m a year") and a source line, the table is sourced, and every figure carries a unit. What stops it at 4 and stops me sending it is density at the two ends of the document. Page 4 is the worst offender: the Assumption box, one H2, a single long paragraph and a Notes-and-sources list with exactly one entry occupy roughly the top 45% of the page, leaving more than half the final page blank — the document trails off rather than lands. Page 1 has the same problem in the other direction: the title block, subtitle, date and confidentiality line sit in a thin band at about one-third height with the entire lower two-thirds of the cover empty and no cover artwork, mark or supporting device. Page 2's second section ("Fund the dispatch decision on day one") is also an unbroken wall of prose describing a three-phase sequence that would have been far better served by the milestone table treatment already used on page 3. Fix the last-page stub, give the cover something below the rule, and it is close.

Integrity holds: no clipping or overflow, the Tier table that breaks between p3 and p4 repeats its column headers on p4, and the chart, KPI trio and timeline table all render fully. Legibility is fine — single measure, dark text on white, headers/footers consistent. Coherence is real: the same blue is used for the cover rule, the three KPI figures on p2, the section rules, the chart bars and the table header rules, and the section-title treatment repeats identically on p2, p3, p4 and p5. Communicative effectiveness is where it earns level 4 — titles conclude rather than label ("What the book actually looks like", "What we expect to cost us in churn", "The two largest accounts, if they refuse"), Figure 1 on p3 carries both a takeaway caption ("tracks unpriced cost inflation, not a change in what customers are shipping") and a source line, the tier table on p3/p4 states share of book, uplift, current vs modelled margin and an expected-churn range per tier with units on every figure, and the p4 callout justifies cost-indexation rather than leaving it implicit. The p5 refusal playbook answers the brief's hardest ask concretely (escalate, trade value-for-value, partial with a revisit date, live contingency). It stops short of level 5 on craft: the tier table splits so that only the Tier 1 row sits at the bottom of p3 with Tier 2/3 orphaned onto p4 — a human would have pushed the whole table over; the cover on p1 is a rule, a title and two small lines with the lower two-thirds empty; p2 ends in a long unbroken block of body copy after the KPI row; p5 stops around two-thirds down; and there are small stray marks at block boundaries (top of the p2 body, above "The nine-month runway" on p4, above "The two largest accounts" and "Recommendation" on p5) that look like leftover anchor glyphs. Not generic in content — the tier/churn table, the nine-month milestone table and the refusal playbook are specific to this book — but the visual system (single column, blue rules, one bar chart) would transfer unchanged to any other advisory memo.

Integrity holds: no clipping, no placeholder text, no overlap — the 'Margin by Account Segment' table on p3 and the 'Expected Churn by Repricing Tier' table on p4 both fit their measure, and the page-3→4 break falls between the churn narrative and its table rather than through it. Legibility is fine: single dark-navy-on-white column, one measure throughout, obvious top-to-bottom order. Coherence is consistent — the same rule-under-heading treatment on p2 ('Three years without a reprice…', 'The book splits into three distinct pricing problems'), p3 and p4; the same running header and the same footer triple (Confidential — Commercial Director / n·4 / September 9, 2026) on every interior page; the two aside boxes ('Segmentation method' p2, 'If either account says no' p4) use identical framing. Communicative work is the strongest part: every heading is a conclusion rather than a label, the p3 KPI row carries units and deltas (19 ▼ -12 pts, 22 ▲, 34 –), both tables carry a source line beneath, the churn table gives a rate per tier as the brief asked, and p4 closes with a numbered Notes and sources block. What keeps it off level 5: it is a wall of prose and two tables — a document whose whole argument is a three-year slide from 31% to 19% and a tiered churn tradeoff has no chart anywhere, so the reader has to reconstruct both curves from sentences; the p1 cover places the eyebrow/title/subtitle block in the top third and leaves the remaining two-thirds entirely empty with no footer or closing mark; and p4 ends its content around 60% of the page height. Genericness: the navy-rule-and-grey-body chrome, the boxed callout and the KPI triplet are stock report furniture — swap the words for a supply-chain or headcount review and the pages would look identical.

Integrity and legibility hold: nothing is clipped or empty, the four pages carry consistent headers ('Pricing Review: Restoring Margin Discipline'), footers with 'Confidential — Leadership Only' and page numbers, and the heading/rule system repeats identically on pages 2-4. Where it stops short is level 4. For a brief built entirely on movement in numbers (31%→19% margin, 22% cost rise, three tiers, churn per tier) the document contains exactly one small table on page 3 — three rows, Below cost / Near breakeven / Top 15% — and no chart at all; the margin decline and the churn ranges that are the point of the review are delivered as prose ('15 to 20%...', 'closer to 5 to 8%' at the top of page 4) rather than as a comparable visual or a churn-by-tier table, which forces the reader to reconstruct the comparison the recommendation rests on. Section titles also label rather than conclude: 'Why This Review Now', 'Expected Churn by Tier' and 'What the Book Looks Like' name the topic; only the tier table's source line ('International-level P&L; sorted, FY2024 trailing twelve months') and the 90days/6mo/9mo stat trio do the work of asserting anything. Rhythm slips in two places: 'Expected Churn by Tier' on page 3 sits at the very foot of the column with two lines under it before breaking, and the page-1 cover leaves the lower two-thirds empty under a four-line block. Visually it is a competent but stock business memo — blue rule under the cover title, ruled headings, one boxed 'Method note' / 'Contingency' callout style, one table; strip the specific numbers and this same shell would serve any consulting review, which is what keeps genericness high despite genuinely brief-specific content.
